question: What type of drug name describes the exact molecular structure of a medication?
explanation: The chemical name provides the precise atomic and molecular description used primarily during laboratory research and development. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h1)

question: Why is the generic name considered the official nonproprietary name for a medication?

options.A: It describes the exact atomic formula needed to synthesize the compound
options.B: It is chosen by commercial companies to boost market sales in different countries
options.C: It is assigned by official bodies and used universally regardless of the manufacturer
options.D: It remains exclusive to the very first pharmaceutical laboratory that discovered it

explanation: Generic names are nonproprietary titles designated by global or national health authorities so the active ingredient remains standardized. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h1)

question: What common suffix do beta-blocker medications share in their generic names?
explanation: Beta-blockers commonly share the generic suffix -olol, which helps clinicians quickly identify their drug class. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h2)

question: How do shared generic stems help nurses during clinical practice?

options.A: They allow quick identification of a drug class and its general mechanism of action
options.B: They dictate the specific physical color and shape of the tablet or capsule
options.C: They indicate the exact financial cost of the medication in retail pharmacies
options.D: They guarantee that two different medications are manufactured by the exact same company

explanation: Recognizing standard suffixes in generic drug names enables nurses to anticipate therapeutic effects and potential class-specific side effects. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h2)

question: What legal protection is granted specifically to a pharmaceutical brand name?
explanation: Pharmaceutical companies protect their proprietary trade names by registering them as official commercial trademarks. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h3)

question: A patient reports taking Panadol for a headache, but the prescription requires paracetamol. What is the relationship between these two terms?

options.A: Panadol is manufactured by the government while paracetamol is imported
options.B: Panadol is a brand name and paracetamol is the generic active ingredient
options.C: They represent completely different medications with unrelated pharmacological actions
options.D: Panadol is the chemical formula and paracetamol is the proprietary trade name

explanation: Brand names like Panadol are commercial labels given to the underlying generic active drug substance, which in this case is paracetamol. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h3)

question: Which of the following is typically true regarding generic drugs compared to brand-name drugs?

options.A: Generic drugs contain different active ingredients.
options.B: Generic drugs are generally much cheaper.
options.C: Generic drugs are legally prohibited from changing color.
options.D: Generic drugs require extensive marketing budgets.

explanation: Generic medications cost less because manufacturers do not carry the initial research, development, and heavy marketing expenses of brand-name developers. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h4)

question: Why might two tablets containing the exact same active ingredient look completely different in size and color?

options.A: One tablet contains a higher concentration of the active therapeutic chemical
options.B: Brand-name drugs do not contain any excipients or binding agents whatsoever
options.C: Different manufacturers use varying inactive binders, fillers, and colorants
options.D: The government alters the physical appearance of medications every single year

explanation: While the active ingredient remains identical, different companies use their own inactive excipients, resulting in distinct shapes and colors. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h4)

question: What term describes when a generic drug shows the same rate and extent of absorption as the brand version?
explanation: Bioequivalence proves that a generic preparation delivers the active drug into the bloodstream comparably to the original branded product. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h5)

question: Why do regulatory agencies like NAFDAC enforce strict bioequivalence testing for generic medications?

options.A: To guarantee that generic drugs achieve the same therapeutic blood levels as brand names
options.B: To calculate the exact retail profit margin for local community pharmacies
options.C: To ensure that every pharmaceutical company uses the exact same packaging color
options.D: To prevent foreign companies from exporting medical equipment into the country

explanation: Enforcing bioequivalence ensures that patients switching from a brand-name drug to a generic alternative receive safe and predictable therapeutic results. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h5)

question: What is a major risk when patients take multiple medications containing the same active ingredient under different brand names?
explanation: Taking multiple commercial products that share the same active generic ingredient can easily lead to dangerous cumulative overdoses. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h6)

question: A patient arrives at the ward taking a branded pain reliever brought from home alongside a hospital prescription for paracetamol. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Discard the home medication immediately without checking any product labels
options.B: Switch the hospital prescription to a completely different class of antibiotics
options.C: Check the active ingredients of both preparations to verify if they are identical
options.D: Administer both medications together to achieve faster pain relief for the patient

explanation: The nurse must verify active ingredients to ensure the patient does not receive a double dose of the same pharmacological agent. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h6)

question: Why might a patient become alarmed when refilling a prescription at a local pharmacy?

options.A: The pharmacy is legally required to charge higher prices for generic drugs than brand-name drugs
options.B: The pharmacist alters the prescribed dosage schedule without notifying the attending physician
options.C: The active pharmaceutical ingredient changes completely with every single refill purchase
options.D: The newly dispensed generic pills may look different in color and shape than previous brand supplies

explanation: Changes in physical appearance between generic manufacturers often startle patients who expect their pills to look identical every time. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h7)

question: What is the best way for a nurse to advise a patient who is worried about switching from a costly brand-name drug to an affordable generic alternative?

options.A: Explain that certified generic drugs contain the same active ingredient and provide equal therapeutic effects
options.B: Tell them to double their daily dose of the generic drug to make up for lower quality
options.C: Insist that they must borrow money to continue purchasing only expensive brand-name products
options.D: Advise them to stop taking the medication entirely if they cannot afford the brand name

explanation: Reassuring patients about bioequivalence and active ingredient identity builds confidence in affordable, regulated generic therapies. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T8#GNS125_U1_T8_h7)
